demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Rajendra Patel's eyes still scan the horizon with a mixture of habit and unease. A retired Coast Guard officer, he spent decades navigating treacherous waters, but it was one fateful accident that left an indelible mark on his life. While responding to a distress call, Rajendra inadvertently caused serious injury to another sailor. The memory of that day remains fragmented – disconnected pieces that refuse to coalesce into a coherent narrative. As he recounts the event, Rajendra's voice falters, and he forces himself to focus on the positive aspects of his life. He tells himself that it wasn't as bad as everyone made it out to be, or that it didn't really happen at all – a coping mechanism he's employed with increasing frequency since the incident. However, these attempts at positive reframing only provide fleeting solace. When sirens pierce the air, Rajendra is instantly transported back to that day, and the memories come flooding back in vivid detail. The sounds, sights, and smells are so real that it feels like he's reliving the event all over again. Rajendra has grown increasingly avoidant of unfamiliar places, always opting for familiar routes and locations where he can assess potential dangers more easily. He's also developed a habit of taking unnecessary risks, almost as if trying to prove to himself that he's still in control. This need for control extends to even mundane activities like choosing his seat – he always selects the one that offers the most protection or the best vantage point. Talking about the future is another trigger that sets Rajendra on edge. It's as if the very prospect of looking ahead fills him with a sense of foreboding, and he begins to ruminate on all the ways things could go wrong. Being in natural environments similar to where the accident occurred also serves as a potent reminder, stirring up memories and emotions that he'd rather keep suppressed. As Rajendra navigates his daily life, these triggers continually reignite the cycle of negative appraisals that have taken hold of his mind. He's convinced that there must be something fundamentally wrong with him – that the accident happened because of some inherent flaw in his character. This self-doubt fuels his hypervigilance, as he becomes increasingly preoccupied with potential dangers and threats lurking around every corner. In an attempt to break free from this cycle, Rajendra has started to push these thoughts out of his mind, trying to suppress them altogether. However, this only serves to further entrench the memories, making them more difficult to access when he tries to recall them deliberately. As a result, Rajendra finds himself stuck in this never-ending loop – perpetually avoiding triggers that threaten to bring back memories, memories that reinforce negative appraisals, and negative appraisals that drive him to employ maladaptive strategies. As the weight of these maintaining cycles becomes increasingly unbearable, Rajendra has finally sought help. He's hoping to find a way to break free from this suffocating pattern and learn to live with himself again. But for now, the sirens continue to haunt him – a constant reminder of that fateful day, and the memories that he can't seem to shake.
